title: Bounded convergent division by finitely many Tate series
statement:
Let $K$ be a field [def-weil-field] complete for a real-valued nonarchimedean absolute value, and let $s\ge0$. Let $T_s=K\langle X_1,\ldots,X_sangle$ be the restricted-series ring [def-trf-restricted-series-presentation], with Gauss norm $\|\sum_
u a_
u X^
u\|_G=\sup_
u|a_
u|$. Order $\mathbf N^s$ by graded lexicographic order: compare total degree first and then lexicographically. For $0
e u=\sum a_
u X^
u\in T_s$, let $L(u)$ be the largest exponent in this order among the finitely many exponents with $|a_
u|=\|u\|_G$. Let $t\ge0$ and let $b_1,\ldots,b_t\in T_s$ satisfy $\|b_i\|_G=1$. For every $f\in T_s$ there are $q_1,\ldots,q_t,r\in T_s$ such that $f=\sum_{i=1}^t q_i b_i+r$, $\|q_i\|_G\le\|f\|_G$ for every $i$, and $\|r\|_G\le\|f\|_G$. Moreover, if the coefficient of $X^
u$ in $r$ is nonzero, then $L(b_i)

u$ componentwise for every $i$. The list may be empty, in which case $r=f$; no assumption that the $b_i$ form a Gröbner basis is made.

proof.text: If $t=0$, take $r=f$. If $s=0$ and $t>0$, then $T_0=K$ by [lem-trf-restricted-series-gauss-completion]; take $q_1=f/b_1$, all other quotients zero and $r=0$. Since $|b_1|=1$, this has the required bound. Thus assume $s,t>0$. Throughout, coefficientwise scalar multiplication has $\|a h\|_G=|a|\|h\|_G$ directly from the supremum formula, including $a=0$.

proof.text: For each $i$, let $H_i$ be the finite polynomial consisting of exactly the terms of $b_i$ with coefficient modulus $1$, and put $e_i=b_i-H_i$. Restrictedness [def-trf-restricted-series-presentation] makes $H_i$ finite and nonzero: a nonzero restricted family attains its positive supremum, by taking the maximum of the finite set of coefficients at least as large as any fixed nonzero coefficient. All coefficients of $e_i$ have modulus less than $1$, uniformly so: only finitely many have modulus at least $1/2$, and their maximum together with $1/2$ is less than $1$. Consequently choose $0<c<1$ with $\|e_i\|_G\le c$ for every $i$, using finiteness of the list. The greatest support exponent of $H_i$ in graded lexicographic order is $\beta_i=L(b_i)$. Put $V=\{a\in K:|a|\le1\}$. The absolute-value identities show directly that $V$ is a unital subring; every coefficient of $H_i$ lies in $V$, and its leading coefficient is invertible in $V$ because its modulus and that of its inverse are $1$. The chosen order is additive and well-founded: every fixed-total-degree set is finite, and total degree cannot decrease infinitely.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-trf-unit-leading-ring-polynomial-division] over the commutative ring $V$ with the polynomials $H_i$ and this graded lexicographic order, separately to every monomial $X^
u$. Choose once and for all polynomial solutions $A_{i,
u},B_
u\in V[X_1,\ldots,X_s]$ of
$$X^
u=\sum_i A_{i,
u}H_i+B_
u,$$
where every support exponent of $B_
u$ lies in $S=\{\mu: eta_i
leq\mu	ext{ for every }i\}$. Embedded coefficientwise in $T_s$, these polynomials have Gauss norm at most $1$, since all their coefficients belong to $V$. Fixing these solutions on monomials avoids any unsupported claim that arbitrary choices of polynomial division are linear.

proof.text:
Use the completeness and ultrametric inequality of [lem-trf-restricted-series-gauss-completion]. For $h=\sum_
u h_
u X^
u$, define
$$Q_i(h)=\lim_{N	o\infty}\sum_{|
u|\le N}h_
u A_{i,
u},\qquad R(h)=\lim_{N	o\infty}\sum_{|
u|\le N}h_
u B_
u.$$
Both limits exist in $T_s$: differences of partial sums after degree $N$ have norm at most $\sup_{|
u|>N}|h_
u|$, which tends to zero by restrictedness and finiteness of the bounded-degree sets. Each partial sum has norm at most $\|h\|_G$, so the limits have the same bound. Finite sums are linear in $h$; the identical estimates applied to $h-h'$ give $\|Q_i(h)-Q_i(h')\|_G,\|R(h)-R(h')\|_G\le\|h-h'\|_G$. Taking limits of the finite monomial identities gives
$$h=\sum_iQ_i(h)H_i+R(h).$$
Indeed, multiplication by the fixed $H_i$ is continuous by the cited submultiplicative estimate, and the left side is the convergent truncation of $h$. Every $R(h)$ has support in $S$, since each forbidden coefficient is zero in every partial sum and $|[X^\mu](u-v)|\le\|u-v\|_G$. These are explicit Cauchy estimates, not an invocation of an extension theorem.

proof.text:
Starting at $h_0=f$, define recursively
$$u_{i,n}=Q_i(h_n),\quad v_n=R(h_n),\quad h_{n+1}=-\sum_i u_{i,n}e_i.$$
The decomposition just obtained and $b_i=H_i+e_i$ give the exact identity
$$h_n=\sum_i u_{i,n}b_i+v_n+h_{n+1}.$$
By [lem-trf-restricted-series-gauss-completion], $\|h_{n+1}\|_G\le c\|h_n\|_G$, since each $\|u_{i,n}\|_G\le\|h_n\|_G$ and $\|e_i\|_G\le c$. Induction from $h_0=f$ therefore yields $\|h_n\|_G\le c^n\|f\|_G$ and $\|u_{i,n}\|_G,\|v_n\|_G\le c^n\|f\|_G$ for all $n\ge0$.

proof.text:
Set $q_i=\lim_N\sum_{n<N}u_{i,n}$ and $r=\lim_N\sum_{n<N}v_n$. These limits exist by [lem-trf-restricted-series-gauss-completion]: for $M>N$, the norm of either corresponding tail is at most $c^N\|f\|_G$, by repeated ultrametricity, and this tends to zero since $0<c<1$. Completeness puts the limits in $T_s$. Summing the exact identities from the preceding step telescopes to
$$f=\sum_i\Bigl(\sum_{n<N}u_{i,n}\Bigr)b_i+\sum_{n<N}v_n+h_N.$$
Letting $N\to\infty$ gives $f=\sum_iq_i b_i+r$: the finite products converge by submultiplicativity, and $\|h_N\|_G\le c^N\|f\|_G\to0$.

proof.text: Each finite partial sum defining $q_i$ or $r$ has norm at most $\|f\|_G$ by the same ultrametric inequality [lem-trf-restricted-series-gauss-completion]; passing to the limit preserves this bound. Explicitly, if a limit had norm greater than $\|f\|_G$, choose a partial sum whose distance to it is smaller than that norm, and the ultrametric inequality gives a contradiction. Every $v_n=R(h_n)$ has support in $S$, so each forbidden coefficient of $r$ is the limit of zeros; coefficient evaluation is continuous because its absolute value is bounded by the Gauss norm. This proves the required remainder condition for all $i$. No uniqueness or Gröbner-basis property was used, and $f=0$, trivial absolute values and nondiscrete value groups satisfy all estimates unchanged.
